extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematics educators, and cognitive scientists studying explanation and understanding
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for when a mathematical proof (or other mathematical object) counts as explanatory, combining philosophical accounts (Steiner, Kitcher, Lange) with a functional/cognitive account of explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steiner’s characterising properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs are explanatory if they make critical use of some ‘characterising property’, defined to be those properties unique to “an entity or structure mentioned in the theorem, such that from the proof it is evident that the result depends on the property” (Steiner 1978).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Gauss’s proof of the sum 1+2+...+n is explanatory because it turns on symmetry properties of the sum; a standard induction proof is not explanatory under this criterion. Advantages: accounts for visual proofs (characterising properties often visualisable) and for the ability to generalise proofs by deforming the characterising property. Criticisms/anti-patterns: counterexamples exist where supposedly explanatory proofs lack identifiable characterising properties, or where proofs meet the characterising-property condition but do not seem explanatory (Resnik & Kushner 1987; Hafner & Mancosu 2005). The account therefore may not be exhaustive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kitcher’s unification (patterns of argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of an explanation is to unify a group of different facts or concepts into a single theory; explanations can be compared by their ‘patterns of argument’: how ‘stringent’ these argument patterns are and how many conclusions they yield. Better explanations use fewer, more stringent patterns to draw more conclusions (Kitcher 1981).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationally: favour proofs that exhibit strong unifying argument patterns—fewer distinct argument forms with greater generality produce more explanatory power. Example: Darwinian unification across phenomena. Criticisms: concrete examples in mathematics show that comparing number/strength of argument patterns can give rankings inconsistent with practitioners’ judgements of explanatoriness (Hafner & Mancosu 2008).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lange’s salience / feature unity
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanatory proof exploits a feature of the theorem’s premises that is salient in the theorem’s result; explanatory proofs reveal a hidden symmetry or a property that treats every relevant instance in the same way (feature unity) (Lange 2014).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proofs revealing symmetry behind equal probabilities in coin-toss examples; the calculator-numbers/divisibility-by-37 example where the explanatory proof identifies a shared property rather than brute-force enumeration. Limitations: difficulties when reasoning about hypothetical but unproven statements (e.g., claims about what P ≠ NP would explain) and other counterexamples noted in the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wilkenfeld’s Functional Explaining (FE) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: “Explainer B explains (engages in an explaining-act with respect to) proposition p to audience A if and only if B produces a representation R that, when properly internalized, causes improved understanding of p in A (where the content of that understanding is similar to R), and B intends to explain or cause understanding via this production” (Wilkenfeld 2014).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key components stressed by the authors: (1) FE is neutral with respect to which account of understanding is adopted; (2) explaining is an intentional act between explainer and audience (can be self-explanation); (3) representations must be 'properly internalised' (avoids counting miraculous or non-standard routes to understanding); (4) FE does not directly require veridicality—whether explanation must be factive depends on the underlying account of understanding. Use FE as the defining criterion: an explanatory proof is one that (in the relevant context) causes improved objectual understanding in an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanations must generate objectual (not merely propositional) understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the functional/epistemic approach explanatory status depends on generating objectual understanding: grasping relations among items of information and forming well-organised schemas (Kelp 2016; Kvanvig 2003).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectual understanding admits degrees (distance from 'maximal understanding'); contextual thresholds determine whether a degree suffices to call it 'understanding'. This distinguishes mere knowledge-that from deeper, schematised comprehension necessary for a mathematical explanation to count as explanatory under FE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directing attention / facilitating selection into working memory
rubrics_metrics.description: A good mathematical explanation has features that make it easy (or as easy as possible) to select the information from sensory memory into working memory that is necessary for successful processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical markers: use of signaling, clear highlighting of conceptually important parts, structured presentation. Cognitive rationale: reduces irrelevant load and focuses limited working memory capacity on the relevant elements (Mautone & Mayer; Mayer & Moreno). Anti-pattern: proofs that bury the key idea in long irrelevant technical detail, making selection difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitating coordination with prior schemas and reorganisation into coherent schemas
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory proofs make it easier to integrate the new information with existing schemas retrieved from long-term memory, enabling reorganisation into coherent new schemas that can be encoded back into long-term memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational cues: analogies to familiar structures, explicit mapping to known concepts, highlighting dependencies and relations. Cognitive rationale: schema theory—experts have well-organised schemas; explanatory proofs help build or refine these schemas. Anti-pattern: proofs that remain isolated from prior knowledge or do not indicate how they connect to familiar structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Splitting working-memory load across visual and verbal/auditory channels (dual-channel design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good explanations distribute processing between visual and verbal channels so the chance of exceeding working-memory capacity is minimised (dual-coding/dual-channel assumption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design guidance: mix diagrams and verbal explanation appropriately (avoid redundant overload in a single modality). Empirical support: mixing auditory and visual presentation can reduce cognitive load and improve learning (Mousavi, Low & Sweller; Mayer & Sims). Example: a visual proof accompanied by descriptive text can be more persuasive/comprehensible than the visual alone (Inglis & Mejía-Ramos 2009). Anti-pattern: lengthy dense prose with no visual support or, conversely, a diagram with no helpful verbal guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualisability and use of visual proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Visualisable characterising properties and visual proofs are often explanatory because they make salient the dependencies and cue the schemas needed for understanding (Steiner; empirical support noted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'proofs without words' that reveal structure visually. Caveat: visual arguments may be persuasive without being fully explanatory in the cognitive sense unless they are properly integrated with representational content that can be internalised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalisability / deformability of proofs via varying characterising properties
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanatory proof, on Steiner’s account, can often be generalised by varying the characterising property; deforming the proof in analogous ways yields an array of associated theorems and proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational test: can the key idea be adapted to produce related results (e.g., Gauss’s approach to sums extended to even numbers). Limitation: Lange and others note proofs that seem explanatory yet do not admit such deformation, so generalisability is not a necessary condition under the functional account—rather it is one property that correlates with explanatoriness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metacognitive detectability of understanding (introspective report as evidence of explanatoriness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under FE, judges often diagnose explanatoriness by comparing their level of understanding before and after reading a proof; individuals have some metacognitive access to increases in understanding (Schraw & Moshman 1995).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use: metacognitive reports can be empirical evidence about whether a proof generated understanding. Caveats: metacognitive judgments are fallible (Goos 2002; Schoenfeld 1985); false positives/negatives (sense-of-understanding, 'aha' feelings) can occur, so combine with other cognitive measures where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic vs ontic account distinction as evaluative lens
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between ontic accounts (explanatoriness is an objective relation independent of agents’ understanding) and epistemic accounts (explanatoriness defined by the explanation’s capacity to generate understanding in agents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for evaluation: epistemic/functional approach requires demonstrating that a proof generates understanding in some relevant audience; ontic approaches must explain why objective features produce understanding (Friedman’s challenge). The paper argues for an epistemic/functional stance but discusses how ontic features (characterising properties, unification, salience) may be mechanisms that tend to generate understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory features as correlates not definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The features identified by Steiner (characterising properties), Kitcher (unification), and Lange (salience) correlate with explanatoriness because they make it more likely a proof will generate understanding, but they do not define explanatoriness on the functional account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical interpretation: when evaluating proofs, treat these features as heuristics or predictors of explanatory efficacy rather than as necessary-and-sufficient conditions. The functional account unifies these features by showing how each aids cognitive processes involved in generating understanding (selecting information, integrating schemas, managing cognitive load).
